balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For FirstService Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For FirstService Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For FirstService Corporation: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For FirstService Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For FirstService Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For FirstService Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For FirstService Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For FirstService Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For FirstService Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For FirstService Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: Residential vs Brands
segmentRevenue.content:
FirstService reports two segments: FirstService Residential, North America's largest manager of residential communities (HOAs, condos), and FirstService Brands, a portfolio of franchised and company-owned property-services brands (California Closets, Paul Davis Restoration, CertaPro Painters, First Onsite, Roofing Corp of America and others).

For FirstService Corporation: Brands has grown faster than Residential for most of the last decade, largely through acquisition (tuck-unders and platform deals), and overtook Residential in absolute revenue around FY2019-2020 -- the mix shift is the central story behind the group's growth rate and its M&A-heavy capital allocation.

What to watch:

  • Whether Brands' growth is organic or bought (compare with AcquisitionSpend)
  • Residential's revenue is contractual and stickier but structurally slower-growing
  • Interim rows show Brands' seasonality (storm restoration, exterior-services weather dependence)

segmentEbitdaMargin.title: Segment Adjusted EBITDA margin: Residential vs Brands
segmentEbitdaMargin.content:
Segment Adjusted EBITDA margin is each segment's Adjusted EBITDA divided by its own revenue -- the profitability of the two businesses on a comparable basis, independent of their very different sizes.

For FirstService Corporation: Brands has run at a meaningfully wider margin than Residential (Residential is a lower-margin, high-volume managed-services business; Brands carries franchise-royalty economics on top of its company-owned operations), so the segment mix shift toward Brands has been margin-accretive for the group, not just revenue-accretive.

What to watch:

  • Margin compression in either segment after a large acquisition (integration costs)
  • Residential margin is the more stable, lower-beta of the two
  • A widening margin gap means the mix shift is improving group profitability, not only growth
